text: I. The messenger came to Shatili: – The Kists have harmed us, they have ravaged our shepherds, wicked, evil-minded ones.

Aluda Ketelauri is a man of fortune,  
he sits at the head of the council,  
his word is wise and well-directed;  
he has cut off the right hand of many a Kist,  
he has tested the sharp French blade.  
Why should one seek enmity with the bad?  
It is always better to be with enemies than with the good!

The Kists have driven off the horses, Aluda’s too, with feathers.  
He has a hunch they’ll sweep over the mountainous head of Arkhoti,  
and shake with hoofbeats the dew-covered street of the mountains.
When Aluda heard this, he intended to fire the gun; he strapped on his weapons, he sharpened the sword; he checked the scabbard, so the sword would not break the hilt.

It is the time of dawn; the falcon of the cliff is swiftly pursuing the enemy.  
At daybreak, in the ravine, the partridge rang out like a bell,  
while the dogs still sleep on the slope, and the sheep have not yet been let out.
“– Aren’t you hurt, you dog of a heathen?! – Mutsali was saying. – Don’t think I’m hurt, you dog of a heathen, servant of the Gudani Cross. The sound of Aluda’s gunshot was like thunder in the sky.”
“Didn’t it hit you, you cursed dog?” — he keeps calling out to him again.
– Mutsal is not hurt, you dog of a heathen, he was clearing away the rock fragments…
– Oh, his hat has a hole in it, and it is brushing against the hairs of his beard.
– You slipped too high, poor fellow; the stone has no bone. Mutsal’s gun went off, the bullet makes a sound in the swift one, it will break Khetelauri’s horned face-shield.
“– Aren’t you still in trouble now, you faithless dog?” – he even reproaches him for that.

– It is not afflicted, no, you law-dog, the vassal of Gudani’s Cross;  
the victorious cross follows him, and he entrusts his strength to God.  
It did not strike the heart, do not suppose; it was breaking the medicine pouch.  
Once it comes to the shooting, I too shall not swallow the enemy’s spite.

The shot from Shatili breaks the Kist’s breastbone.  
— Aren’t you in pain even now, you cursed dog of a faith?! — he shouts at the Kist.
– It pains me in my heart, in my heart, you lawless dog, alas for Mutsali’s trial! You have killed my brother too, kill me as well; what can I say to God’s grace?

Mutsal does not wish for death,  
he does not lose the color of a wolf;  
he tears and tramples,  
they lie in the wound, the mountain grass.  

Aluda fired once at him,  
he does not lose the moment of his trial.  
He threw Aluda’s rifle back too,  
and says one more word to him:  
– Now let it be yours, you lawless dog,  
may it not fall into another’s hands.

His words dried on his lips, and he stretched out on the ground. Aluda did not want the rifle; he wept like a woman. He does not seize the weapons, his eyes do not covet them. He laid the dagger by his head, with its ivory hilt; he placed the breastplate upon his chest, and the French sword upon his arm. He does not cut off the right hand of the slain man; he would say: “It would be a sin; brave man, slain by me, may God give rest to your dead soul. May your right hand rest upon your arm, it is not unjust to you; may your own hand lie upon your heart, may the stone gate never rejoice, you have had a good nurse, may God bless your lineage!” He spread the cloak lengthwise and laid the shield over it.

The ibexes have climbed the glacier, the grace of God has settled upon their horns.  
From ravine to ravine the raven croaks with an evil voice:  
“Psh, the Kist Mutsali has died; I must eat the eyes of the lad,  
I must tear out the heart and liver, and cover the shoulder with my skirt.”

Shatili has not yet been reached by the light of the midday sun;  
they do not let the descender in, the sky is covered by the cliff.  

The youth came, hill by hill, his head does not seem to fit;  
mist has settled on his face, drawn from the heart, it is black.  

On the throne hangs the arm of Mutsali’s brother,  
a bazala adorned with silver, that Khurasani sword.  

It is attached to the rocky crag, where the smoke of hope is;  
in summer it watches for the sound of guns, in winter avalanches descend.  

Many times the deluge has overtaken me,  
the black raven was barking.  

The insatiable vulture would flap above his head,  
no one could ruin his fortune, no one could bring him evil.  

The fierce rays of the sun melt even the hands of the unbeliever.  
The snake could not cut through the foundation; even today it is alive.  

Sometimes a storm settles, sometimes the sun shines, there is fair weather.  
What have they done? Many a mustached dead man has been seen!  

Many times the bloodstream of those killed for slaughter has gone forth;  
the evil Ardoti water has turned red.

Whoever thirsts for enmity, let him open the door of his house,  
let blood pool in the hearth, and let him stand there himself.  
Let him drink it as wine, and let it serve him as bread.  
Let him make the sign of the cross, as though he were in a church.  
Let him have his wedding in blood, and there let his cross be written.  
Let him invite guests, and let him line up his troops.  
Let him spread his bed in blood, and let him lie down beside his mate.  
Let him have many children, many sons and daughters;  
and there let him dig a grave, and there let his dead be buried.
If you kill another, you too will be killed; a clan does not spare a murderer.

From Shatili, a Khevsur woman and daughter-in-law came out onto the terraces, and Aluda’s brothers and nephews came out to meet them. Many wanted to hear the story, and many others came as well. They congratulated Aluda:

— May you be renowned!

The old man asks about brave Aluda’s deed of trial. Ketelauri tells the story of the Ghigla wolf:

“Going this way, fearless one, I cut the track of the mountain. I soon overtook him. I trapped his trail in the sand. There were two of them; I used my gun, and I could not reach them with my sword. In that blessed one’s belly, iron had been laid in his heart!

– What are you saying? A Kist’s salvation was not written in the law. – That is why I praise manliness: it cannot be bought with money. I shot three times, he shot three times, and with the third I finished it. The bullet that struck him in the chest tore out his heart. He was covering the wound with his hand, and so he gave up his soul. He would not let the soul leave, and again he remembered the law.

We shall say, “We are men; only our mothers have raised us;  
we shall be saved, while the breathings of the lawless await them in pitch.  
By saying this, we speak in vain; the sons of God know better.  
Do not all speak the truth, indeed, those who swear it?!”

They turned their backs on Aluda with bitter resentment;  
they made for their own homes, with doors and lofts.  
They condemned Khetelauri with hearts full of sorrow and wrath,  
calling out Aluda’s name with blame upon their lips.

Mindi also came to Shatili on a dapple-gray horse with eight bells, with a French sword girded at his waist, with a shield on his arm, and with a twelve-cubit Kist spear in his hand. Mindi’s red forehead, moon-like, was like that of a deer.

They spoke ill of Aluda with poisonous words.  
He was offended, and his brow furrowed with a fearful wrinkle.  
– Do not speak ill of a brave man with a windy tongue.  
May your enemy die easily, and may I easily learn the truth.  
We do not want much sorrow; let one day’s provision be enough for me.  
Let the road and trail not be confused for me; I know the way in every direction.  
Mindia will come to you today, before many have settled down.
He struck his heel, the red one hurried on, moving like a breeze.

The devni come out from the cliff, wandering through the ravines and hollows. Everyone has had supper and is now getting ready for sleep.  
– Have some bread, they say, pleading with Aluda’s mother.  
– I don’t want bread, mother, for some reason my heart feels heavy; last night I had bad dreams, I was somewhere in a line. In front of us lay a dead man, and the Khevsurs sat there in grief. Those prepared for battle, some stood by the gates. I was there too, and I wept, as is proper for a man. I had a feeling of going to war, and the time for departure had come.

In an instant, someone seized my hand and placed the hilt of a dagger in it.  
I looked up: it was Mutsali, wearing a coat of chainmail,  
and on his chest there was a mark from that moment of battle,  
a gray wound from the shot of the enemy’s arrow.  
He stood like a rock, unbroken,  
and no tear fell from his eyes.

“I want to die, but I do not die; kill me,” he said pleadingly. “Let the world remain yours, and I will depart from this land; be satisfied, children of Khevsureti, with campaigning and with the waving of swords.”

I sat down, a bowl was set before me by someone; it was juicy with human flesh, I was eating it, though human hands and feet were bony and it disgusted me. What was I doing? I was grieving, disgraceful, accursed.
“Eat, — Ramam called to me, don’t stand there stunned: serve me Aluda’s broth and meat, reheated.” They added broth and meat seasoned with a man’s mustache…
I am tormented by dreams; that is what is troubling my mind.

IV. Dawn breaks, the mountain peaks turn red, and mists gather upon the mountains.  
The village rises and wakes, and travelers come and go along the roads.  
The pines set out on the crossroads, and cast their eyes over hill and dale;  
how many are in the fluttering throng, yet they have left no trace in the sky!
“Who comes riding on the red horse, has he crossed the water? — You have come in peace! — the Khevsurs call out to Mindia. — What news have you brought? — they call from afar.”

– Young men, your blood is boiling; you cut and sew with your hearts, you let your hearts be dragged by your minds, you let your heads be chopped off with an axe, and you cannot easily recognize a man by his manly code! Do not let one another be oppressed; the heart and the mind are brothers. Aluda is right; may the heavens not fall on my head! If you do not believe it, Kist, here is the severed arm. Keep your tongue in its sheath; do not speak words lightly, do not speak lightly of a man, saying, “He is no good!” He extends the hand to Aluda: “Take it, place it by the stone!”

– If I had wanted to cut off a hand, why would I not have cut off my own?  
I cannot do you good, Mindia; I will finish your affair badly.  
Why do I need it? It does not call to me; it will not serve as a shield.  
If I take it to the mountains, it will not mow, nor will it be useful as a scythe.  
Take it away, if you believe in the Lord; do not show it to me again.  
It is the right hand of a good man, and my heart burns with guilt.  
Why are the Khevsurs angry, why are they breaking with grief?!  
I will kill the enemy, but I will not cut off their right hand by force!  
“It is not proper to kill an enemy if you do not cut off his hand with a knife.”  
Woe to such justice, baptized in sin and guilt!

V. The time of the Lord’s feast had come. The people were going to the icon festival: they had to inform the lord of anyone who was in pain. Men and women gathered with offerings of sheep and oxen; they would present their offerings to the lord through the barn door.

Who is this that has come, like mist, with a finely wrought brass sword?  
He gives the mountain elder a bull, and stands there with bowed head.

– Whom are you making an offering to, Aluda, with this black bull? – the priest asks Aluda, with his arm outstretched. Our lord is great, with the Gudani Cross at his head, and he has strong vassals too, by God and by God’s power. Our lord loves a good vassal; he grants favors abundantly. Brave men, full of hope, place their trust in our lord. Tell me the name of the one to whom you are offering it, and let it be offered to him. – He draws his dagger, ready to speak of glory.

– That is the mourning cloth, Berdia, of the Kist man killed earlier. They called him Mutsal, the son of the unbaptized one. Bless me well too, you have doomed me for him, just as for the beautiful brother of the one who was unwillingly killed.

– You are correcting the faithless, but that does not suit you; it does not befit you to slaughter a sacrificial animal for the Kists. An inheritance does not come from a father, nor from a grandfather, nor from a great-grandfather; come to your senses, you are a Christian, and by this you are becoming faithless; do not follow the devil… how did that word escape your lips?! How many others have you killed, their hands hang on your neck like claws, some are Lezgi, others Kist, a bridge of the right-handed; you have not even slaughtered a kid for anyone, let alone a bull. How can I beg the Lord for a dog, a dog of that breed? Better that the heavens collapse on me, that the earth split open beneath my back, or that the boundless sea swallow me, so that I may eat a meal of sand! Berdia is turning pale, the color of a different kind of fear.
“– You are trying in vain, Aluda, in vain you wear out your mouth.”

Ketelauri grew furious, like a wolf in color;  
He struck with his French sword, and the sun’s light burst forth.  
He swung at the bull upon the neck, and its head rolled down below.  
Then he pleaded with the lord: do not pity my son,  
Let his belly be laid waste, that unbaptized hero.

Berdia Jagarashlili will turn his face against the people. – It has been heard, – he was saying, – thus is the casting off of the faith: Aluda himself slays the sacrificial victim, I call upon the soul of the Kist, people, I want to hear the answer of your hearts. Gather yourselves, sons of the Khevsurs, all of you — great and small, let us do justice, let us break Aluda’s house posts; do not spare them, let them become the weepers of wife and child. Let it be cut off, the sky-and-cloud watchers of another land. Go, break the black-dark doors of the house, the fortress gates. Set fire to the barn, — let the flames reach the sky, drive out the sheep, cows, and bulls for the community. Make Shatili’s wife and children weep, Gudani’s — the old women and girls; let our lord be angered, there is no pity for him.

Hearing this, Mindia’s eyes filled with tears,  
Aluda can no longer be helped,  
he folds his arms across his chest,  
the sons of the Khevsurs, enraged, raise their shields,  
Ketelauri must be made to know;  
the copper plates ring harshly.  
The Khevsurs, seated as an army, were overtaken by the children,  
one of them had seized in his hand  
the bones of his right arm, broken at the joint.

– O noble one, I strive to obtain for you the lord’s mercy; hide the precious treasure, and I will bring you the enemy’s hand. The raven was carrying it with its talons, steering toward the cliff’s cove. At that moment I boldly shot an arrow at the one soaring through the sky; the shot proved true, and it struck the raven’s wing. With its claw it let go of the prey, and it fell to the ground.

– The right side of Mutsal, the reason for the Khvsurs’ counsel, – Mindiya would say in anger, – the reason for their curse; I brought it to Aluda, I laid on it the color of offense; when Aluda did not accept it, I showed him the depth of the gorge.

– Take it, – says Berdia, – the branch of the godless dog; are we not the sons of the Khevsurs, servants of the devil, Alisa? They will throw to the dog to eat the hand of Mutsal’s arm. Let the cur not come near; he set up a howl of guilt.
Khevisber Berdia says: – Khevsurs, see with your own eyes: a dog does not break another dog’s bone, it is said from the same source. The children of the Kist drag the right hand down with a hook.

VI. Snow is falling, the wind is raging, the necks of the mountains are bound;  
The avalanches of the cliffs are coming down into the ravines.  
The skirts and hems of the waters have been sewn together in blue by the ice,  
The narrow paths have been entirely covered over.

Whoever has grown weary of life, who will set out on the road?  
The traveler goes ahead, he blazes the trail, and five follow behind him.  
Tormented by hunger, the pack of wolves howls on the mountain.
“Do not look for anything good, Khevsurs,” one woman said in anger. “Alas, our home and hearth, stone no longer stands upon stone; now crows are sitting on the fortress, on the pillars of the loft.”

Mother would say to Aluda:  
– My son, walk slowly, for neither I nor your wife Lela can endure you; the children have grown restless, and it has chilled our hands and feet. Alas, how roadless we wander, alas, how dark it is! Would that the Khevsurs would not need your help?! What stream or meadow will receive us, where shall we spend our days? Homeless, without hearth or house, we have become accursed even elsewhere. We can no longer reach our home and hearth, beyond the Shatili gorge. To give up one’s native land has proved far too hard; I have become like one half-dead, my mind turned to madness. My knees no longer carry me, and in my heart a dark pillar has been set. Ah, graves of father and forefathers, cliffs standing sharp and steep!

Aluda says angrily:  
– Women, do not be so talkative; come, follow me, let us go. God has granted this to us as our fate. Do not offend the cross, do not curse the community, do not turn into fools!

Once Aluda turned around, once he turned his head back:  
“Farewell, you cliffs of the pasture, joy of my eyes!  
Farewell, my home and hearth, you who stir guilt within my heart!  
Farewell, our lord, you who give power to us servants!”

They have forever forsaken the travelers’ water and their own land.  
The mountain peaks stand dumbly, the wind’s whistling is heard.  
They crossed over, they passed the ridge, no trace of the ditch is seen.  
From afar, May’s bitter sobbing of a woman.
